clue.text: Newspaper drops last part of report about important match

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the shortened paper is read backwards
drops means the newspaper's name loses a letter, here the one named next

parts.note: The Times is the newspaper that publishes this very crossword

indicators.note: the last part of a word is its final letter, taken from the word report

explanation.surface: A paper cuts the ending of its report on a big game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drops last part of report' takes T off TIMES to leave IMES; 'about' turns that round.
explanation.definitionFit: A semi-final is a crucial match that decides who reaches the final.

clue.text: Cringing from an extremely creepy Psycho production

indicators.note: a production of a film is a new staging, so the letters are remade in another order

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters, from creepy

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A remake of the Hitchcock film Psycho is fawning and creepy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' gives CY from creepy; 'production' shuffles AN, CY and PSYCHO.
explanation.definitionFit: Sycophancy is servile flattery, cringing behaviour towards the powerful.

clue.text: Mime artist brought up memory thus for listener

indicators.note: in a down clue brought up means read from bottom to top

parts.note: RAM is computer memory

indicators.note: for listener means the word for thus is heard, not spelt

parts.note: so means thus or in this way

explanation.surface: A mime remembers what happened, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: The French ending CEAU is pronounced like SO.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcel Marceau was the world-famous French mime artist.

clue.text: Wrongly promoting smart officers can lead to grudge

parts.note: fly is British slang for sharp or knowing, so smart
POs are petty officers in the navy
a can is a tin

indicators.note: the lead to a word is its first letter, here from grudge

explanation.surface: Unfairly advancing clever officers may lead to resentment in the ranks.
explanation.walkthrough: Fly-posting is the British practice of sticking up advertising bills illegally, hence promoting wrongly.
explanation.definitionFit: Fly-posting is advertising by putting up posters without permission, an illicit form of promotion.

clue.text: Form of transport in Seoul failing to cover a single mile

indicators.note: to cover means the rearranged letters go round the next pieces
failing suggests something collapsing, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder
taken as written as anagram fodder
a single is one, I as a Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A vehicle in Seoul breaks down before covering a mile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'failing' turns INSEOUL into LOUSINE, which 'to cover' wraps round IM.
explanation.definitionFit: A limousine is a large luxurious car, a form of transport.

clue.text: Models sets of bloomers one can wriggle out of

indicators.note: wriggle out of means escape from, so the letter leaves the word

parts.note: posies are small bunches of flowers, bloomers being flowers
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Models wearing bloomers one could slip out of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloomers' suggests underwear but means flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: To pose is to model, so poses are what models does, verb to verb.

clue.text: Politicians indicate where speaker might sit when bill is introduced

indicators.note: is introduced means the bill goes into the word for indicate

parts.note: to show is to indicate
an ad is a bill or advertisement
a loudspeaker sits in a cabinet

explanation.surface: MPs show where the Speaker sits when a bill comes before the House.
explanation.walkthrough: 'speaker' suggests the Speaker of the Commons, but it is a loudspeaker. The shadow cabinet is the opposition's team of senior politicians in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The shadow cabinet is a group of opposition politicians who mirror government ministers.

clue.text: One thousand newspaper reporters strike

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
the press is journalists collectively

explanation.surface: A thousand journalists walk out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strike' suggests industrial action but is the verb meaning to make an impression.
explanation.definitionFit: To strike someone as clever is to impress them, a shared sense of affecting the mind.

clue.text: Crossing Ardennes, taking in one region of France

indicators.note: taking in means the phrase before holds the answer within it

explanation.surface: A route through the Ardennes passes through part of France.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the end of 'Crossing' and the start of 'Ardennes'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gard is a département of southern France, named after its river.

clue.text: Garment is seen in church (Catholic church, mostly)

indicators.note: seen in means the word is sits inside what follows
mostly means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: the Roman Catholic church is often called simply Rome
taken as written

explanation.surface: A piece of clothing spotted in a Catholic church.
explanation.walkthrough: Rome stands for the Roman Catholic church; 'mostly' drops its last letter and 'seen in' signals the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: A chrisom is the white robe put on a child at baptism, an old church garment.

clue.text: Bob grasps wooden coffin lid — spooky

indicators.note: grasps means holds, so the coin word goes round the other pieces

parts.note: bob is old British slang for a shilling, a pre-decimal coin
pine is a wood used for furniture and coffins

indicators.note: the lid of a word in a down clue is its top letter, from coffin

explanation.surface: Someone clutches a pine coffin lid in a scary scene.
explanation.walkthrough: A shilling was a British coin before 1971, nicknamed a bob.
explanation.definitionFit: Spine-chilling means frightening, causing a shiver down the spine, so spooky.

clue.text: Rouge etc for every scarlet woman!

parts.note: slap is British theatrical slang for make-up such as rouge
per means for each or for every

explanation.surface: A painted lady's make-up spending, item by item, exclaimed over.
explanation.walkthrough: A slapper is British slang for a promiscuous woman; slap is greasepaint or cosmetics.
explanation.definitionFit: Slapper is a crude British slang term for a promiscuous woman, a modern scarlet woman.

clue.text: Diamond, perhaps pure one? Cost is ridiculous

indicators.note: ridiculous suggests something absurdly out of order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder
taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Is a perfect diamond worth its absurd price?
explanation.walkthrough: 'ridiculous' rearranges PUREONECOSTIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A diamond is one example of a gem, signalled by 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Eg dinner prepared with it

indicators.note: prepared suggests food being made up, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder
taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A dinner, for example, is made with this.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: a dinner is prepared with each component.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingredient is one of the foods combined to prepare a dish or meal.

clue.text: Grave: a French accent

definitions.meaning: the rising mark over an e in French, as in café

explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'grave' a second accent beside it, but here it means serious.
explanation.definitionFit: Acute means severe or critical, and the acute is also a written French accent.

clue.text: Strongly influences boy following instance of naughtiness?

indicators.note: following means the boy comes after the first piece

parts.note: an imp's act is a mischievous deed, read playfully as one word
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: A lad's mischief has a big effect on others.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: an imp act is a piece of mischief.
explanation.definitionFit: To impact on something is to affect it strongly, a common modern phrasal verb.

clue.text: A trail through holy area in part of S America

indicators.note: through means the first pieces run inside the holy area

parts.note: pi is informal for pious, so holy
to tag on is to trail behind

explanation.surface: A trail passes through a sacred site in South America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'through' puts ATAGON within PI and A.
explanation.definitionFit: Patagonia is the southern region of South America, shared by Argentina and Chile.

clue.text: Pet I buried in container is most likely to be remembered

parts.note: a cat is a common household pet

indicators.note: buried in means the letter I is put inside the container word

parts.note: a chest is a large box for storing things
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pet's ashes sealed in a box are what one remembers longest.
explanation.definitionFit: The catchiest tune is the most memorable one, the superlative of catchy.

clue.text: Yank enjoyed embracing English blonde

parts.note: to yank is to pull or tow

indicators.note: embracing means the word for enjoyed holds the letter for English

parts.note: had means enjoyed, as in had a good time

explanation.surface: An American enjoyed hugging an English blonde.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yank' looks like an American but is the verb to pull.
explanation.definitionFit: A towhead is a person with very fair hair, so a blonde.

clue.text: War hero gave command to leader of regiment

parts.note: bade is the past tense of bid, to order

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, here from regiment

explanation.surface: A military hero issued orders to the regiment's commander.
explanation.walkthrough: Douglas Bader was a famous British fighter pilot of the Second World War who flew despite having lost both legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Douglas Bader was a celebrated RAF ace, a national hero of the Second World War.

clue.text: Complaint in seaside resort

indicators.note: resort read as re-sort means sort again, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An illness caught in a beach town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort' looks like a holiday place, but read as re-sort it rearranges SEASIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint is an illness, so disease is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Lies on ward with leg broken; orderly required

indicators.note: broken suggests something shattered, so the letters are put back in a new order

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder
taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A patient lies in hospital with a fractured leg, needing an orderly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'orderly' looks like a hospital attendant, but it is the adjective. 'broken' rearranges LIESONWARDLEG.
explanation.definitionFit: Orderly and well-organised are synonyms: both describe something neatly arranged.

clue.text: Bigger than usual crossing worried Antarctic explorer

indicators.note: crossing means the size letters go over and around the word for worried

parts.note: OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize
ate means worried, as in what's eating you

explanation.surface: An outsized man crossing the ice made a worried explorer.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Lawrence Oates died on Scott's 1912 return from the South Pole.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence Oates was a member of Scott's ill-fated Antarctic expedition.

clue.text: Problem about copyright for dirty film?

indicators.note: about means the problem word goes around the copyright letter

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem
C is the symbol for copyright

explanation.surface: Copyright trouble over a blue movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dirty film' suggests a pornographic movie but means a layer of grime.
explanation.definitionFit: Scum is a film of dirt or froth on the surface of a liquid.

clue.text: Early sign of cold? He has spray

definitions.text: Early sign of cold? He has spray

indicators.note: the early sign of a word is its opening letter, here from cold

parts.note: taken as written
a mist is a fine spray

explanation.surface: When your cold starts, here is someone with a nasal spray for you.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: the pharmacist is who you visit with a starting cold, and he stocks sprays.
explanation.definitionFit: A British chemist is a pharmacist, who sells remedies such as nasal sprays for colds.

clue.text: Maybe almond covering for fruitcake

parts.note: an almond is one example of a nut
a case is a covering or casing

explanation.surface: Almond shells for a fruitcake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fruitcake' suggests baking, but it is slang for a crazy person.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruitcake and nutcase are both informal words for an eccentric or crazy person.

clue.text: Islander's crazy to have a container filled with petrol

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, so the definition is the islander alone

parts.note: mad means crazy

indicators.note: filled with means the fuel goes inside the container phrase

parts.note: a can is a metal container
gas is the American word for petrol

explanation.surface: An islander is mad enough to carry a can full of fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Islander's' reads as 'Islander is', the 's being a link; 'filled with' signals the fuel going into a can.
explanation.definitionFit: A Madagascan is a native of Madagascar, the large island off south-east Africa.

clue.text: Relish extract of lemon?

definitions.meaning: relish means gusto or keen enjoyment
the outer peel grated from a lemon is used for flavour

explanation.definitionFit: Zest means enthusiasm, and it is also the grated rind of citrus fruit.
